rounds.name: Tech Round 1
rounds.description: The round began with the typical “Introduce Yourself” question. It is important to plan this thoroughly, as it often sets the tone for the rest of the interview. A well-structured introduction can guide the flow of the conversation toward your strengths and areas you are most comfortable discussing. While introducing yourself, try to subtly highlight any project/internship/competition that might catch the interviewer’s interest. In my case it was a website which I had made for my father’s company which automated a lot of repetitive tasks. The interviewer was curious about the same and we went on to discuss it for a couple of minutes. Next, I was asked to code the classic string permutations problem. Always make sure to explain your thought process and dry run for the same first then start coding. Even while coding, explain each line as you are typing. Then we had a discussion about some of my other projects in my resume and the interviewer questioned me for my choice of the tech stack for each of them. The interview concluded with me asking two non-technical company related questions.

tips.text: MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor, as most students were able to fully solve the DSA and SQL questions.Focus on practicing MCQs extensively, especially during the final phase of your placement preparation.
Always make sure to go through the types of questions a company has asked in previous years. This proved to be very helpful for students who had done so for this OA :)

If you're unable to think of an optimized solution right away, start with a brute-force approach or use the hit-and-trial method. The goal is to pass as many test cases as possible within the limited time, even if the logic isn’t the most efficient initially.
Make sure you have ample sleep before the day of the interview as it is going to be a very long day ahead.

In case you are asked a question which you have seen/solved previously, do not make the mistake of directly jumping onto the optimized solution. Start off with the brute force, then go on to explain how you would improve your code to get the most optimal solution possible. You do not want the interviewer to know that you are already aware about the problem.

If you are stuck on a question, first explain your approach to the interviewer and ask for hints afterwards. Most of the time, they are interested in your thought process and how well you are able to communicate and understand the problem.
Have 2-3 unique projects which you can talk hours about. Have the what, why and how prepared for each project ready. It is always a plus if you’ve worked on a project with real world impact.
Try to use SQL databases as many times, you might be asked to discuss the schema designs.
Research about the company values beforehand and try to answer the questions organically in a way which aligns with them, for Barclays, these included RISES principles
Thoroughly explain your thought process for decision-making questions, including how you weighed the pros and cons in each scenario.
Try to ask good questions at the end of the interview.This is to ensure that the interviewer remembers you throughout the process
Your communication skills matter a lot during the interview. Practice thinking out loud while solving DSA problems
A well crafted resume can help you right from shortlisting to the final HR round. Aim for an ATS score of 70+ on platforms like Resume Worded
Luck plays a quiet but powerful role during this season.Sometimes, despite giving your all, it slips away; other times, it finds you when you least expect it.

Gear up for a potential emotional roller coaster, bound by anxiety, fear, hope(lessness), and joy at last. This phase of life will teach you a lot, make sure to learn from every rejection. All you need is one good day. Sooner or later, if you’ve prepared sincerely, that day will come.
Make sure to participate in Hackathons (and Case Study Competitions if you are preparing for PM/IB/DA roles). They are a great way of developing good projects and learning new things.
If you're preparing for a non-tech role, evaluate whether you can also do at least basic DSA preparation in parallel. It proved to be one of the best decisions in my case.
If you don't get selected, don’t be disheartened there’s always another company and another chance. Stay focused, stay hopeful, and keep moving forward.

tips.text: Make sure to go through previous years' OA questions; the coding question may be repeated.
Brush up on Java theory and basic DBMS/OOPS concepts.
SQL basics (especially filtering rows using WHERE and logical operators) should be known.
Practice DSA regularly using Striver's A-Z sheet to improve speed and accuracy.

Strengthen Your Core Subjects: Ensure you have a strong understanding of Computer Science fundamentals like OOPS, DBMS, OS, and CN. Many of the MCQs in the OA round and questions in technical interviews are directly based on these concepts.
DSA is Crucial: Practice coding questions regularly. Completing Striver’s A-Z DSA sheet is highly recommended. It will help not only for the OA but also for the technical interviews.

Java Concepts: Since Java is a preferred language in many companies (including Barclays), you should know about its internal workings. Learn about JVM, JDK, JRE, memory model, autoboxing, generics, garbage collection, lambda expressions, comparators, TreeMaps, etc.
Aptitude Practice: Don’t ignore aptitude. Practice questions from IndiaBix and PrepInsta. They’re helpful for logical reasoning and quick decision-making.

Competitive Programming: While not mandatory, doing CP improves your problem-solving speed and ability to think under pressure. Start with the CP-31 sheet by TLE Eliminators. Try solving questions on platforms like CodeChef, CodeForces, and LeetCode regularly.
SQL & DBMS: Basic SQL questions can be game-changers. Make sure you know how to use SELECT, WHERE, AND, and basic joins. Also, revise normalization, indexing, ACID properties, and ER diagrams.
Behavioral Round Prep: Be honest. Your attitude and ability to work in teams matter just as much as your technical skills. Interviewers can detect fake responses.
Stay Consistent & Positive: Placement season is stressful. Not clearing a test or getting rejected after interviews is normal. Don’t compare your journey with others.
Luck plays a role too, from the question you get in OA to which interviewer panel you face. Focus on continuous improvement.
Stay Connected: Build a peer group that supports and motivates each other. Help your friends and ask for help too.
Final Word: Never lose hope. Everyone gets placed at their own time. What matters is persistence and faith in your own abilities.

rounds.name: Technical Round
rounds.description: My interview began with a brief introduction round. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, followed by questions about my family background, CGPA, and whether I was satisfied with my college and academic performance so far. Next, he asked me about my primary programming language, to which I responded Java. He then asked a simple DSA question on finding duplicates in an array. He handed over his laptop and asked me to code the solution in as many ways as I could. I first implemented the solution using a HashSet. After that, he asked me to make a few variations in the code, which I successfully implemented. Following that, the discussion moved to Java concepts and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). The interviewer then focused deeply on Exception Handling in Java. He: Asked several questions, ranging from basic to advanced level. Requested me to code examples using try-catch-finally blocks directly on his laptop. Asked about different types of exceptions, their behavior, and expected outputs. Also made me predict the output of the code I had written, then verify it by running the program. While coding and answering, I made a few minor mistakes, but nothing major. The interviewer seemed okay with them, so don’t stress too much over small slips. Lastly, we discussed one of my projects, where I gave an overview and explained the problem statement, tech stack used, and key features. At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his role at Barclays and the technologies he works with.

tips.text: It’s never too late to start. Whether you’re in first year or already into third, what matters is starting today. You’ll thank yourself later.

Choose your primary programming language and stick to it. Be it Java, Python, or C++, master one language thoroughly. But also have a basic understanding of other popular languages, especially if they come up in interviews or MCQs.
Start DSA preparation seriously.
Keep 1–2 strong, impactful, and preferably unique projects in your portfolio. Projects that solve real problems, demonstrate initiative, or use newer technologies really help you stand out.
Don’t ignore your core Computer Science subjects like DBMS, OS, CN, OOPs, and SQL. These come up a lot in interviews—both technical and MCQ rounds.
Participate in extracurriculars! Being active in committees, hackathons, and competitions not only builds your confidence but also shows that you're a team player and proactive.
It’s okay to face rejection. I had tests and interviews where I didn’t make it before this offer. But remember: every failure teaches you something, and you only need one "yes."
Keep your resume updated and tailor it for each company. Highlight relevant projects, achievements, and internships.
Mock interviews help. Practice with friends or seniors. The more you simulate the pressure, the better you’ll perform.
Always stay consistent — even if you can only study or code for an hour a day, it adds up.
And finally, never stop believing in yourself. Confidence and self-belief are game changers.

tips.text: My selection was largely due to my ability to stay calm under pressure, even when faced with questions I couldn't fully answer.
My honesty about my limitations, coupled with explaining my approach or conceptual understanding, showed integrity.
My detailed preparation in OOPS, Java, HTML, React, SQL, and DBMS fundamentals was crucial, especially since MCQs were a deciding factor in the initial round.
In the HR round, being confident, truthful, and demonstrating problem-solving skills with practical reasoning helped immensely.
Engaging the interviewer and asking relevant questions also showed genuine interest and initiative.

My biggest learning from this experience was the need for thorough practical application of concepts, especially in areas like SQL procedures and triggers, beyond just theoretical understanding. It's crucial to not only know what a concept is but also how to implement it with code or queries.
I primarily practiced MCQs from GeeksforGeeks to strengthen my foundational knowledge in OOPS, Java, C++, Objective-C, SQL, and DBMS.
For coding, I focused on problems from LeetCode.
I focused on preparing OOPS, Java, SQL, and DBMS concepts in depth.
Ensure your resume clearly highlights your projects, particularly showcasing your role and contributions, and the technologies used.
Be prepared to discuss every detail mentioned on your resume, as interviewers will cross-question. Don't include anything you're not confident about.
Regardless of how challenging the questions get, maintaining your composure is key. A small, calm smile can convey composure and confidence. Don't give up, even if a round feels like it went poorly.
Always have a pen and paper handy for jotting down thoughts or working through problems.
Keep your phone screen facing downwards to avoid any distractions.
Sit straight, maintaining good posture, as it reflects engagement and confidence.
Strive to make the interview a two-way conversation, engaging with the interviewer. Think out loud while solving problems; it helps the interviewer understand your thought process.
If you don't know an answer completely, it's better to honestly confess and explain what you do know or how you would approach finding a solution, rather than bluffing.
At the end, always ask thoughtful questions about the role, team, company culture, or expectations. This shows genuine interest.
By keeping these points in mind, and remembering to stay confident and true to yourself, you can significantly improve your chances during the placement process.

The MCQ section focused mainly on Java fundamentals, especially OOPs concepts. Many questions included code snippets, where we had to guess the output. The questions were quite tricky and concept-based, so a strong grip on the basics really helped. The SQL part was relatively easy—just a basic query where we had to use a WHERE clause along with an AND condition.

tips.text: Ensure that you are really clear conceptually with OOPs, as different MCQs had differing weightages attached to them. MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor as most students could solve the DSA question and SQL query fully.
Apart from SQL50 on LeetCode, ensure to familiarize yourself with basic String and Date functions and their syntax in SQL.
Master your OOPs concepts — a majority of the questions came from this area.
If you know the right answer, be confident. Sometimes interviewers may challenge you on purpose just to test your conviction.
Know your resume inside out. Don’t include anything just to fill space — if it’s on there, be ready to discuss it.
For coding problems, always start with the brute force approach. Then discuss how you can optimize it.
Keep talking through your thoughts during the coding part. Don’t go silent. The interaction matters as much as the solution.
it’s really important to be aware of Barclays' RISES values and try to include them naturally in your responses to situation-based questions.
Preparing some standard HR questions in advance helps a lot, especially if you can back up your answers with real stories.
It's also important to interact with the interviewer—don’t just turn it into a Q&A session. Try to make it a discussion.
Stay attentive, because small things happening around you can give you the spark for a clever or memorable answer—but make sure you don’t get distracted.
whatever your strengths are, try to reflect them—directly or indirectly—throughout the interview.

paying attention during the PPT (Pre-Placement Talk). Some of the things discussed there—especially around the company’s work culture, Barclays’ values, and the tech stack they use—came in handy during the HR and project discussion parts. So I’d strongly suggest taking notes during the PPT, because it can give you useful context and even points to connect during the actual interview.
Prepare well, trust your luck, and enjoy the journey — it teaches you a lot about handling stress and managing time.

This was a long and drawn out process, and intern and grad interviews were ongoing at the same time. The interviews started at 10am after the PPT, and my interview was finally conducted at 3:30pm. It went on for around 30 mins. The interviewer started off by testing me on my knowledge of Java & OOPs. Then moved on to 2 easy level DSA questions. Then moved on to projects on resume.

rounds.name: Techno HR round
rounds.description: After 2 hours of anxiously wondering if my name would be called or not, I was called in for the next round. The interview started off with him asking me to introduce myself. This led to him starting off with a scenario based problem where he introduced a bug in my project. He then asked me to design the schema of the project. He then basically gave a scenario where referential integrity of a foreign key was being violated. He then gave a scenario based question based on the project, where a junior disagreed with a certain part of the implementation. We then had a discussion on polling vs queuing. He then asked me if I knew what Binary Search was, its time complexity, and showed me a simple function with a double for loop and asked me for its time complexity. He then asked me if I was comfortable with python. He then gave me an example about Java object comparison. He also asked me about PostGreSQL vs MySQL. Lastly, I was asked another situational question. Some people had this round as a purely HR round, others Techno-HR round.

tips.text: Ensure that you are really clear conceptually with OOPs, as different MCQs had differing weightages attached to them. MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor as most students could solve the DSA question and SQL query fully.
Apart from SQL50 on LeetCode, ensure to familiarize yourself with basic String and Date functions and their syntax in SQL.

At first glance, the questions seem really basic and straightforward. However, how you decide to answer the question and how in depth you go with the explanation lets the interviewer know about your critical thinking skills, how you analyze a problem and how much of the topic depth you are aware of.

Interview rounds really are a test of your mental strength. Try not to worry too much if your interview is happening late, my interview was last on my panel and only lasted 30 mins compared to other interviews which went for an hour and above. I had mentally given up hope since it had been 7 hours of just sitting and waiting, and some students had started with their round 2 while I hadn't even given my round 1. Such situations might be inevitable, so try not to focus on areas that are out of your control. But try not to let it affect your mindset in the interview, just focus on giving your best performance.

Ensure that you really know your projects inside out. It's not necessary to be able to reproduce the code, but you must be aware of the logic and be prepared to justify your design choices. You may ask any LLM to generate relevant questions based on your projects to gain a better understanding of scalability and differing implementation methods.
It's always better to say I don't know over giving a wrong answer.

Your introduction really sets the tone for the interview, and allows you to navigate through the topics you want the interviewer to probe you on. I hadn't even planned on including the last line, it was just something that spontaneously came up in my head and I just said it. I would advise against this - as the interviewer may ask you questions you are unprepared for.

Even if your project is relatively simple, think of making it a complete product. This includes handling edge cases, how your system is designed to scale, and a secure user experience. My main project scope was really simple, but there were enough technical details to discuss with the interviewer because of the extensive tech stack and how I designed the system.
An obvious tip but do keep RISES in mind whenever you're answering any situational questions. Also, prepare scenarios where you demonstrated RISES just in case you're asked about it.
Apart from just knowing your projects inside out, try to think of edge cases your application might encounter, how you prevent abuse of the system, and how you would scale the system.
Try to deploy your projects and know about what AWS is and how it works. I was asked about it, but I was unaware.
Have 2 good projects you can explain, but I was barely asked anything about my third project.
Be prepared to justify the tech stack used for the project.

Learning to face rejections will be an important part of the process. Before Barclays, I faced rejections in my Trilogy interview and my Incred interview. I could not clear OAs for PhonePe, MSCI, EDS, UBS, IDFC.

50% of the process depends on your preparation and the other 50% on luck. The panel you get may ask you questions from topics you aren't familiar with, be honest and open to learning. I was lucky that I was asked a lot about my primary language, java.
Barclays uses Java a lot so it's advantageous if you have projects in springboot or have a strong hold over core Java concepts.

I cannot overstate how big of a factor luck is during placements. I had a streak of bad luck in my OAs before finally getting the offer from Barclays. I only got to start the test in the last 30 mins out of the total 75 minutes in my MSCI OA due to technical issues with my link.

Don't underestimate the importance of having good projects on your resume, I neglected dev skills and that was the reason I was rejected in my Trilogy interview. Learning from this mistake, I created my main project which I was ultimately asked quite a bit about in my Barclays interview.
Try to not let the factors that are out of your control affect the factors that you can control.
You already know the usual, be clear with fundamentals of OOPs, DSA, DBMS, know how to write SQL queries, and be familiar with the technicalities of your mentioned frameworks.

The discussion then moved toward the project section, focusing on three Full Stack MERN projects: Zerodha, Job Portal, and StudyNotion. The round concluded with the candidate asking questions about roles, responsibilities, and the interviewer's role.

rounds.name: Techno + HR Round
rounds.description: This round was a mix of technical and HR-based questions. The interviewer went through the resume and asked about JWT authentication, including its structure (payload, header, signature), expiry, purpose, and storage location (client/server side). A discussion around cookies also took place. HR questions included how the candidate learned multiple programming languages, an incident of misunderstanding and its resolution, contributions to group projects, hackathon experience, and an experience of teaching/mentoring, including details about getting into teaching and JEE Advanced percentile. The round concluded with the candidate asking a question about learning new technologies at Barclays.

questions.text: What exactly is JWT?
what does "expiry" mean in JWT, is it set by default or manually, what is the main purpose of JWT, and whether it is stored on the client side or server side.
how I learned multiple programming languages.
Have you ever misunderstood anything? If yes, what action did you take, and what was the conclusion?
what contributions I had made in my group projects and about my hackathon experience.
Have you done anything in your life whose fruits are still being enjoyed by someone?
how I got into teaching just after giving my JEE Advanced exam, and also asked what my percentile was.

tips.text: have faith in yourself and in your efforts. If you’ve worked hard, it will pay off sooner or later. Rejections are part of the process, and luck does play a role. What matters most is giving your best every single time, regardless of the outcome.
Start preparing for core CS fundamentals and OOPs concepts 2 to 3 months in advance. Even though I code in C++, I prepared OOPs in Java specifically for such assessments.
Practice the SQL 50 sheet on LeetCode thoroughly. Also, review window functions, as they are commonly asked in interviews.

Begin DSA preparation at least 6 months before placements. I am more inclined toward DSA and competitive programming, so I maintained a daily streak on LeetCode and participated in contests. It’s not mandatory to do competitive programming on platforms like Codeforces, but it definitely helps.
make sure to come early and be on time.
While attending, make sure to note important points like their values, culture, company’s Tech Stack, RISES principles, etc.
Make sure you know your resume thoroughly because they can ask anything and everything from it.
It's always a good idea to ask company-relevant questions to show your interest.

Don’t get stuck in the DSA vs. Development debate. Strive to maintain a healthy balance between both. While DSA and CP build problem-solving skills, in interviews your projects and CS fundamentals often take center stage.
Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.0 to ensure eligibility for most on-campus companies. No matter how skilled you are, missing eligibility criteria due to CGPA can be disheartening.
Core subjects like OOPs, DBMS, OS, CN, and SQL are crucial. These are frequently asked in interviews and can make or break your performance.
Get familiar with basic system design concepts. I was asked about this in my PhonePe HM round, so don’t ignore it.
Be fluent in at least one programming language—C++ in my case, but Java or Python are equally good. Depth matters more than breadth here.
Have at least two solid and unique projects in your resume that you can explain thoroughly and confidently. Your ability to discuss them can drive the interview forward.
Regular participation in CP contests sharpens your thinking under pressure and builds speed—both essential in coding rounds.

Do your best, be consistent, and give every opportunity your 100%. Remember, luck also plays a role on interview day. Don’t get disheartened by rejections—keep going. Opportunities will come; just stay calm, hopeful, and focused.

rounds.description: The online assessment consisted of a total of 15 questions and had a duration of 1 hour and 30 minutes. Among these, one was a DSA problem of medium to hard difficulty, and another was a relatively easy SQL question. The remaining 13 questions focused on Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs) and SQL concepts. It’s important to pay close attention to the weightage of the MCQ questions, as each question carries a different number of points. Make sure to solve the higher-weightage questions carefully, as they can often be the deciding factor in your overall score and selection. The OOPs questions, generally asked in either C++ or Java, require a strong foundational understanding of core OOP concepts. As for the SQL MCQ’s, although the questions were on the easier side, they still tested your understanding of key concepts like GROUP BY and JOINS.

tips.text: While explaining my projects, I made a conscious effort to relate them to real-world scenarios—highlighting the actual problems people face and how my project aimed to solve them. This approach helped the interviewer understand the practical impact and relevance of my work.

During the explanation of various technical concepts, I used numerous examples to illustrate each point, which helped convey my in-depth understanding clearly. I didn’t just explain what I used, but also why I used it, why I chose it over alternatives, and how it benefited the project overall. This demonstrated not only my technical depth, but also my thought process and problem-solving mindset during the development phase. It also reflected my genuine passion for building meaningful projects and thinking through every detail.

One of the most important things to remember during interviews is not to get intimidated by the interviewer. They’re not there to scare you — they’re there to evaluate you, yes, but also to help you bring out your best. Keeping your mind calm is crucial. When you’re relaxed, new ideas, better explanations, and clearer thought processes naturally flow. That’s when you’re able to think on your feet, connect concepts, and frame your answers effectively.

I would highly recommend adopting a similar approach when discussing your projects—if your interviewer is open to hearing your thought process. In my case, the interviewer was specifically interested in understanding the reasoning behind my decisions.

That said, it’s equally important to read the interviewer’s expectations. If they prefer direct, to-the-point answers, then align your responses accordingly. Adapting your communication style based on the interviewer’s cues can significantly enhance the impact of your responses.
